videos.title: Oklahoma City leaders narrow data center moratorium after debate
videos.description:
The debate over new data centers in Oklahoma City intensified as the City Council voted to narrow a temporary moratorium and clarify which projects must follow the restrictions.

Council members spent hours debating how far the moratorium should go before approving a more limited version.

Councilman Matt Hinkle of Ward 5 said the city is not trying to stop development, saying, “We’re not killing data centers. We’re being a worthy investigative body on how they will affect our city.”

Hinkle also said he sees the issue as one of governance and oversight, not opposition to the industry. “If they don't build it here, they're going to build it in Piedmont or Hydro or or or or or. And so I'm not against data centers, but I'm not for data centers. I'm for good governments in Oklahoma City,” he said.

Ward 2 Councilman James Cooper raised concerns about exemptions and said he has heard worries from students, including about artificial intelligence.

“I hear regularly from my students existential concerns. About their water supply, their electric supply, but almost above and beyond that, artificial intelligence, AI. They're concerned about when they graduate right now. Will their jobs be there?” Cooper said.

Some council members, including Hinkle, supported what was described as “Option 2,” which addressed concerns about water usage. Hinkle said, “There's not a single bit of water that comes out of Oklahoma City's water supply that's going to be spent cooling any of those systems, which is responsible operations as far as i'm concerned.”

Ward 7 Councilmember Camal Pennington said he supported the approach because it still requires projects to go through the city’s standard review steps.

“I'm comforted by the fact that it doesn't exempt these data centers from having to come back before us for review, for zoning, or for permitting. So the fact that we're just saying you're just going to have to go through the regular process which allows the public to be heard is a comfort to me in this,” Pennington said.

The council voted 7-2 for Option 2. The temporary moratorium remains in place but will apply only to large-scale data centers, with other projects and sites exempted.

Under the revised approach, the moratorium will now impact data centers using more than 75 megawatts of net electrical load.

The two largest proposed data center projects were also deferred, meaning they will return to the council for another discussion and vote.

videos.title: Oklahoma City leaders place moratorium on data centers
videos.description:
Oklahoma City leaders say they need more time before allowing new data centers to be built within city limits.

On Tuesday, the Oklahoma City Council approved a temporary moratorium on new data centers within city limits.

Officials say the moratorium prevents the acceptance of new applications, the processing of, and the issuance of rezoning requests and permits related to the construction or expansion of data centers.

“The temporary pause on new data centers will give the City more time to understand how they affect our community's resources such as energy use, water demand and land use,” City Manager Craig Freeman said. “This brief pause ensures we move forward strategically, so future projects align with our community’s needs and support sustainable, long-term growth.”

The moratorium takes effect immediately and will remain in place until either Dec. 31, 2026, or earlier if amendments to the city's zoning code regarding data centers are approved by the city council.

During the moratorium, the city council will evaluate the potential impacts of data centers and determine what regulatory framework should guide future developments.

Officials say the moratorium exempts two specific pending rezoning cases.

videos.title: Edmond City Council approves data center permit moratorium through December
videos.description:
Edmond leaders hit pause on new data center proposals, approving a temporary moratorium as the city studies how the facilities could affect the community.

The Edmond City Council voted unanimously to approve a moratorium on allowing applications for land or building permits for data centers.

The moratorium runs through Dec. 31, 2026, and includes an emergency clause allowing the ordinance to take effect immediately.

The issue returned to Edmond City Hall after the last meeting at the end of May, with city leaders saying they do not want to permanently block business but want time to research different types of data centers and their potential impacts. “I’ve seen what it's done to communities. It's torn them apart. It's divided them. Anger, and I don't want that happening in Edmond." Edmond Vice Mayor Barry Moore said.

City leaders outlined a research timeline tied to the moratorium.

Research is expected over the next two months on the impacts of data centers and the different types.

In three months, a draft will be presented to the council, and in five months, a final draft will be presented.

During the meeting, a member of an OSU data center research committee offered to research 117 questions about water and energy usage.

“It’ll be titled, Considerations for Communities Evaluating Data Centers,” said Ander Fleet of the OSU Data Center Research Committee.

Not everyone who spoke was opposed to data centers.

Jeff Stokes, who spoke in favor of data centers, said, “We’re running into budget problems; this is a way for us to have some type of tax revenue."

One council member said Edmond is not in a position to house a hyperscale data center but does not want to close the door on smaller ones, citing a belief that businesses with up to 500 employees will all want one within five years.

Ward 4 Councilman Phil Fraim urged a data-driven approach, saying, “Let's make policy out of information and knowledge, not out of fear.”

Near the end of the public discussion, residents raised concerns including water consumption, privacy, eminent domain, and pollution.

Wendy Dial, who spoke against data centers, said, " Forever chemicals, once you get them in the water supply, you cannot get them out.”

Mayor Nash said he has been attending meetings with other mayors across the country for six months to discuss the impacts of data centers.

He said the community will have additional chances to share concerns during four more Edmond Matters sessions.

videos.title: Can Oklahoma Taxpayers Win With Data Centers? Pete Sepp Makes the Case
videos.channel: OKC, Tulsa & Statewide News: Oklahoma Memo
videos.description:
Data centers have faced intense opposition in Oklahoma over their demand for electricity and water, limited transparency and uncertain benefits for surrounding communities.

But could these massive projects ultimately lower property taxes, strengthen local tax bases and generate new economic opportunities?

Oklahoma Memo founder Ryan Welton talks with Pete Sepp, president of the National Taxpayers Union, about the potential financial benefits of data centers — and what communities should demand before welcoming one.

They discuss:

• How data centers can affect residential property taxes
• Whether developers should pay for electrical-grid upgrades
• Why communities need more transparency before projects are approved
• The controversy surrounding tax incentives
• Water use and closed-loop cooling systems
• The number and types of jobs data centers create
• How local governments can negotiate community investments
• Why residents still have the power to say no

Sepp argues that communities shouldn’t automatically accept — or reject — a data center. Instead, residents should demand the facts, scrutinize the costs and determine whether a proposed project genuinely benefits local taxpayers.

videos.title: Texas using loophole to power AI data centers
videos.description:
Data centers are going up all over Texas. But two data centers being built on San Antonio’s far west side are meeting with resistance from homeowners and environmental groups because they're both constructing natural gas power plants and setting up dozens of diesel generators right next to neighborhoods.

The News 4 I-Team investigated allegations that the state is allowing the data centers to side-step pollution safeguards.

Environmental groups claim the state allowed the data centers to use a permitting loophole so they could avoid strict pollution controls and build power plants on-site without notifying nearby homeowners.

“At first I thought it was a medical center, maybe a university building," said homeowner David Thompson.

Thompson says he found out a couple of weeks ago the towering structure being built across the road from his home is a natural gas plant that will provide power for a massive data center owned by a company called Vantage.

“I'm just concerned about the local environmental impact. Were they following regulations? Is it going to be safe for my family, my daughter, who was just born last year?" Thompson said.

Vantage is building two data center complexes.

The one on Omicron Drive next to Thompson’s neighborhood will have two data center buildings, a natural gas power plant, and 86 diesel generators.

A second data center between Rogers Road and Highway 151 will have a similar layout.

Environmental groups say the two sites will produce enough energy to power a city the size of Richmond, Virginia.

“We believe that these are major sources of air pollution and should be appropriately permitted as such," said Kathryn Guerra with Public Citizen, who used to work at the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality.

Guerra says the plants should be treated as major sources of air pollution, which must install stringent pollution controls before building, and engage with nearby residents.

Instead, Public Citizen says Vantage received a minor pollution source permit from the state, the type commonly given to dry cleaners, gas stations and auto body shops..

“San Antonio and Bexar County already have bad air quality that fails to meet the national ambient air quality standards and so this pollution is only going to make it worse for those communities," Guerra said.

Governor Greg Abbott has called for data centers to build their own power plants rather than put a strain on the Texas power grid.

“Any AI data center even thinking about coming here, they got to bring their own money, bring their own power," Abbott said.

The news organization Floodlight shot thermal imaging drone video of a data center in Abilene, which has a natural gas power plant built under a minor pollution source permit.

Environmental groups claim these emissions shown in the thermal image video can contribute to ground-level ozone pollution and contain formaldehyde which can cause cancer.

Public Citizen and the Sierra Club have threatened to sue the Vantage data centers in San Antonio and its partner in building the power plants VoltaGrid. Neither company responded to our requests for comment and so far, TCEQ hasn’t either.

“Companies need to ensure that what they're doing isn't adversely affecting the neighborhoods they're putting themselves into," Thompson said as he held his young daughter in his front yard looking across at the power plant.

Residents will finally get a chance to give their input next month at a hearing as Vantage tries to get its final, Federal Operating Permit.

Environmental groups claim at that point in the process it's often too late to change anything.

videos.title: Oklahoma water demand forecast rises 13% by 2075 but omits data center impact
videos.description:
Oklahoma’s demand for water is expected to rise over the next 50 years.

Still, a new statewide forecast does not account for what officials and experts say could become one of the biggest unknowns: large data centers.

The report projects total water demand will increase from 1.96 million acre-feet per year in 2020 to 2.22 million acre-feet by 2075, a 13% increase.

Agriculture remains the state’s biggest water user.

Crop irrigation accounts for more than half of Oklahoma’s water demand and is projected to increase 14% by 2075.

The second-largest increase comes from public supply.

As Oklahoma’s population grows from about 3.96 million people to 4.76 million, water demand is expected to increase 18%.

Self-supplied domestic use is projected to increase 17%. Industrial demand is projected to increase 10%.

The forecast projects that livestock water demand will drop by 5%, while thermoelectric power demand is projected to drop by 12%.

Oil and gas demand is flat.

However, the Oklahoma Water Resources Board said the projections did not include future demand from new facilities such as data centers.

Matt Cogburn of the Oklahoma Water Resources Board said, “Our projections did not look at what people call hyperscale, larger data centers.”

The Oklahoma Water Resources Board said the state’s water forecast did not include future demand from new facilities that secured water permits because there was no reliable information to estimate their water use.

The report notes 20 industries holding 23 industrial water use permits reported qualifying data to the Oklahoma Water Resources Board and are included in the forecast’s industrial sector, but the water-user data was not included to protect privacy.

Travis Roach, an economics professor at the University of Central Oklahoma, criticized the omission. Roach said, “At the time of this report’s writing, there was already well-reported information of our government trying to extend tax benefits to these data centers entering the state. So, this was either an egregious error to omit this, or it was purposeful.” He added, “I cannot imagine a scenario in which you do not include data center demand in a state’s water comprehensive plan. It’s wild.”

Asked whether people should worry about turning on their faucet and water not coming out in the next 50 years, Cogburn said, “I think it depends on how that data center plans to use water. Again, how that project is designed and how the community’s supplying them with water, looking into the future needs and taking that into account.”

Roach pointed to a potential example in Oklahoma City, saying, “Oklahoma City is considering a data project, and I think it would include about a new 5 million gallons per day water draw. That’s about 5% of our total city delivery. So, any given day the city is providing 100 million gallons per day. So, this is equivalent to taking water away from 75,000 people for a single data center.”

videos.title: Main Street turns into a town hall as Luther faces off over a proposed data center
videos.description:
A week after a packed town hall meeting on a proposed data center was postponed because there wasn’t enough room for everyone, Luther residents gathered again — this time outdoors on Main Street — to weigh in on a plan that has sparked strong opposition.

The earlier meeting was postponed after former lawyer and self-proclaimed journalist Ron Durbin threatened town officials with a citizen’s arrest for violating the Open Meeting Act because not everyone could fit inside the small town hall.

That meeting had more than four hours of speakers, with each person limited to two minutes.

Town Manager, Rian Harkins says the council decided to postpone the meeting because they were at capacity and did not have time to move everyone outside.

A week later, town leaders moved the discussion outside and blocked off Main Street.

The meeting covered a rezoning request, a specific use permit, an infrastructure agreement, and a proposed moratorium related to the data center.

Luther residents June Yarberry-Valuikas and Tony Valuikas sent a letter days ahead of Wednesday's meeting protesting the proposal to the governor and other news stations.

Fox 25 reporter Rob Hagan asked who had reached out. Tony Valuikas said, “Just you."

June Yarberry-Valuikas said she moved her family to Luther because she says her daughter was being bullied at an Oklahoma City school.

She said her daughter has autism and that the community embraced her. “The town of Luther welcomed her. They even made her basketball queen,” June Yarberry-Valuikas said.

Her daughter, Kara Patterson, said she has sensory issues and is afraid of the noise she believes could come with a data center. “I’ll be on overload,” Patterson said.

Tony Valuikas said he spent days researching potential impacts and focused on the area he believes would be affected within a square-mile radius. “It’s 293 properties,” he said.

When asked what Yarberry-Valuikas thinks of when she hears "data center," she said, "Heartbreaking.”

When asked what she thinks of when she hears “data center,” Patterson responded, “We don’t need it. I want Luther just the way it is.”

After the meeting, the City Council passed a moratorium on the data center until Dec. 31, 2026.

The council also decided to take no action on the specific use permit.

The meeting adjourned at 9:50 PM.

Harking said there will be another opportunity for Luther residents to discuss the data center proposal when the moratorium expires next year, but did not specify a date.

videos.title: Luther Town Hall meeting on proposed data center postponed due to overcrowding
videos.description:
More than 100 people packed into Luther City Hall to weigh in on a proposed data center development, but never got the chance to speak after the city council meeting was postponed because the room was overcrowded.

Residents had signed up to address the council over a proposed data center from Beltline Energy.

The company has been proposing data centers across Oklahoma, including in Piedmont and Yukon, and now in Luther.

The meeting’s maximum occupancy is 128, and it was postponed after the crowd exceeded capacity.

Outside, residents shared concerns about the project and how it has been handled so far.

Luther resident Jamie Warner directed a message at the company, saying, “You chose the wrong town, you chose the wrong state.”

Beltline Energy is seeking land for a data center east of the Redbud Power Plant.

Fox 25 obtained a non-disclosure agreement limiting what information has been publicly available about the project’s finances, timing, and plans.

The NDA was signed by the mayor at the end of May a year ago.

Some residents said they are upset they learned about the project after the NDA was signed, including those who recently moved to the area.

Property owner Michelle Mills said, “I’m a brand-new property owner, we haven’t even built our house yet.”

Luther resident Destiny Mowers said, “Anytime you see a data center on the agenda, emotions get high.”

Mowers, who moved to the area two years ago to raise her five kids, said she would be about 300 feet from the proposed data center on 400 acres. “It’s heartbreaking,” she said.

Mowers said she is concerned about environmental impacts and about bright lights from the facility affecting the night sky. “I don’t think we’re going to be able to see the stars anymore,” she said.

Jenni White, who lives 1 mile from the Redbud Power Plant, said she has been fighting a massive transmission line from the substation.

The substation is crucial to help supply power to the data center, and now she is also fighting the data center itself. “Why are the people not being protected? Why is the land not being protected?” White said.

She also suggested a different location for the data center, “What about Tinker Air Force Base? There’s a lot of power, water, and cement.”

Town officials said the NDA requires ratification by the board of trustees.

The dispute resolution states that any dispute must be resolved in writing to Beltline executives at a higher position than the contract signee.

It's unclear what happens next, but residents said they expect another large turnout when the issue returns to the agenda. Mills said, “This is way too important.”

The next city council meeting is scheduled for Wednesday, June 17.

videos.title: Tulsa council launches zoning code review that could reshape rules for data centers
videos.description:
The Tulsa City Council has approved the initiation of a zoning code reevaluation that could change how data centers are regulated within city limits.

The move comes amid growing concerns from council members about the potential off-site impacts of large-scale data center developments, including noise, water usage, and electrical demand.

Currently, Tulsa’s zoning code classifies data centers under “ Industrial Light” or “Low-Impact Industrial,” a designation that assumes little to no impact on surrounding properties. Councilor Laura Bellis (District 4), who brought the item forward, argues that classification may no longer reflect the reality of modern facilities.

“Right now they’re defined as having low or light industrial impact, which means they have no off-site impacts for people or businesses nearby,” Bellis said during the council meeting. “But we’ve learned a lot more in recent years about what these facilities can generate.”

Bellis pointed to instances where companies seeking to build data centers in Tulsa have requested changes to the city’s noise ordinance, something she says indicates developers recognize potential sound impacts.

Tulsa’s current noise ordinance is broadly written, relying in part on what a “reasonable person” would consider a nuisance affecting their wellbeing. Bellis said the concern goes beyond decibel levels and may also include vibration and other operational effects.

To some council members, the rapid growth of the data center industry adds urgency to the review.

“The industry is moving fast,” Bellis said. “If we don’t pause and make sure our zoning code reflects today’s realities, there could be unintended consequences for people who live nearby.”

Public concerns raised during council meeting included questions about long-term water consumption, strain on electrical infrastructure, and the placement of facilities near residential neighborhoods.

Large-scale projects continue to surface across the Tulsa Region. One of the most notable proposals is Project Anthem, an estimated $800 million data center campus planned for east Tulsa.

ALSO: Excitement builds for Project Anthem in East Tulsa

The project remains pending final approval following delays related to zoning considerations and environmental review.

City officials said the current action does not change any rules immediately. Instead, it authorizes the city’s planning office to research potential updates to the zoning code. That process will likely involve reviewing how data centers of varying sizes are categorized and whether larger facilities should be considered “Industrial Moderate” rather than “Industrial Light”

A change in classification could affect where future data centers are allowed to locate, particularly in areas near residential development.

Council members say public engagement will take place once planning staff present draft recommendations. Potential town halls and public hearings are expected before any final amendments are adopted.

Tulsa currently has multiple data centers operating within city limits, most of them smaller facilities. However, officials acknowledge that larger-scale proposals have prompted a reassessment of whether existing regulations adequately address their potential community impacts.

The zoning reevaluation is now in the research phase, with recommendations expected to return to the council in months for further discussion and public input.

When it comes to data center resistance, Oklahoma is ground zero, from Claremore, to Coweta, to Sand Springs, the world is literally watching.

"The overall argument is that the city didn’t follow the proper Oklahoma statutes that are required to meet contiguity requirements in order to annex that parcel into the city limits," he said.

The city told News Channel 8 in part, "we are very confident in the process that has been done to annex the property of the proposed project. We intend to move forward with the zoning process and look forward to a speedy resolution to the meritless claims .“

Schmidt says the attitude of city leaders...

"Has been very abrasive and just non-caring. Their mind was made up a long time ago," he said.

"They started talking about this data center back on March 19th is the earliest we can find and the community didn’t find out about it until early part of November," he said.

With news of the lawsuit he says, donations have started rolling in, as the group taps into a collective frustration many people feel towards the topic.

"Data centers in general right now have a really big problem with transparency and regulation and the lack of regulation that holds them accountable to the people who are going to have to live with the consequences," he said.

Finding a way to fight back in Sand Springs, with residents sending a clear message of, you just kicked a hornet's nest.

"We’re not just a bunch of dumb hicks and ranchers and farmers, there’s a lot of very well-educated, well-connected people and a lot of resources up here that I don’t think they anticipated this level of fight," he said.

"The City of Sand Springs is still evaluating the claims made by the plaintiffs, but we are very confident in the process that has been done to annex the property of the proposed project. videos.title: Sand Springs residents rally against proposed data center, fearing environmental impact
videos.description:
SAND SPRINGS, OKLA. (KTUL) — Residents in Sand Springs went door to door Friday with signs to warn neighbors about Project Spring, a proposed data center they believe could reshape their community.

Kyle Schmidt is the president of the newly formed Protect Sand Springs Alliance. He lives just about a mile from the proposed site and says many people still have no idea what's being planned.

“We feel like a lot of the residents of Sand Springs don’t know what's going on or even anything about data centers,” Schmidt said.

Schmidt says he and others are concerned about the environment and financial impacts, especially regarding water use and the massive power demand data centers require.

“It will have a massive impact on the entire City of Sand Springs, it’s just a lot of people don't understand what that impact is as far as the millions of gallons of water used, massive power consumption that is going to drive up everybody’s electric bills,” Schmidt said.

Earlier this month, a community meeting of about 400 people was held. Residents have also been vocal at city council meetings.

Schmidt said that they recently scored a small win. According to the City of Sand Springs, the developer White Rose Partners has asked to postpone the Dec. 3 planning commission meeting to allow more time for community discussion.

Schmidt runs the alliance's Facebook page and website, where he shares research on data centers, environmental concerns, and potential costs to PSO customers. He mentioned that cheap land and easy access to water are driving big tech companies to build data centers across Oklahoma.

“Anywhere there is cheap land and availability of water, they are moving in, and they are moving in fast,” Schmidt said.

Longtime residents like Lana Compton said they fear what the development could mean for Sand Springs' farming community. Her family has lived here for four generations.

“I don’t want it to be run and lose our animals, our feeding programs, lose all farming,” Compton said.

She mentioned that many neighbors feel blindsided and hopes more people will speak up.

“Please come out and support us. We were not aware of this happening; it was all done underhandedly, and that’s not correct,” Compton said.

For now, the community is using the delay to build support, pushing city and state leaders to be more transparent as the project moves forward.

videos.title: Amazon Walked Away From This County — Then Commissioners Froze Everything
videos.description:
Amazon abandoned plans for a data center campus on the grounds of a Maryland nuclear plant — and within days, the county commissioners who replaced the ones voters threw out passed a six-month freeze on every new data center project. A North Carolina planning board voted to kill a rezoning for the second time. A Wisconsin well-permit hearing ended with the chairman banging his gavel and threatening to clear the room. And new BloombergNEF numbers put the gas plants being built to feed AI data centers at 318 million tons of CO₂ a year. Here's what actually moved.

🪧 COMMUNITY — The Calvert County, Maryland Board of Commissioners unanimously approved a six-month moratorium on new data center projects, days after Amazon abandoned plans for multiple campuses on the grounds of the Calvert Cliffs Nuclear Power Plant. The Amazon proposal covered three campuses across roughly 200 acres — eight data center buildings totaling about 2.4 million square feet with up to 500 MW supplied by Constellation Energy, which operates the plant. Residents first learned of the proposal in February. By the June primary it had become the defining local issue, and three incumbent commissioners who had opposed a moratorium were defeated. The pause gives leaders time to weigh zoning changes or an outright ban.

⚖️ LEGAL — The Stokes County, North Carolina planning board voted 5–2 to recommend that commissioners deny the rezoning behind Project Delta, a large data center proposal near Walnut Cove. It is the second rejection at that stage. Commissioners approved the rezoning in January, but the approval was declared null and void in April after a lawsuit argued the public hearing notice failed to meet state requirements. Developer David Couch submitted a new rezoning application in July. Supporters cite a projected 250 to 500 permanent jobs. Commissioners had already rejected a proposed six-month moratorium on a 3–2 vote, leaving the rezoning as the decisive question.

🪧 COMMUNITY — The Coweta County, Georgia Board of Commissioners unanimously adopted a 180-day moratorium on data center proposals — after having already approved two. The freeze halts acceptance of permit applications, land use amendments, rezonings, conditional use applications, variances and all data center public hearings while the county studies other jurisdictions and drafts a stronger ordinance. The trigger was Project Sail, a $17 billion campus pitched by Atlas Development that ranks among the largest server farms ever proposed in Georgia. Five proposals already filed retain vested rights under state law and are exempt from the pause.

⚡ POWER — BloombergNEF counted 99 gas power projects planned specifically to serve data centers across 22 states, more than a third of them in Texas, representing about 126 gigawatts of on-site generation. Backers include Amazon, Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic and specialized data center operators. At an industry-standard 60% utilization the plants would emit roughly 318 million metric tons of carbon dioxide annually. The entire U.S. electric power industry emitted about 1,485 million metric tons last year, meaning this single slice of infrastructure could lift national power sector emissions by 20% — and by closer to a third if the plants run flat out.

💧 WATER — The Port Washington, Wisconsin Board of Public Works delayed action on Vantage Data Centers' request to use three existing wells on its property during construction of its campus, after residents packed the meeting and demanded the request be denied. The meeting grew contentious enough that chairman Mike Gasper, a city alderman, banged the gavel, called for silence and at one point threatened to have members of the public removed. The board pushed the vote to its next meeting at 5:30 p.m. on August 25, and asked for a timeline and sunset date for well water use, metering information, assurance the well water will not feed the closed-loop cooling system, notification if the wells are modified, and a wastewater testing plan.

🏛️ POLICY — Oklahoma lawmakers marked the signing of House Bill 2992, the Data Center Customer Ratepayer Protection Act of 2026, authored by Rep. Brad Boles, R-Marlow, and Sen. Grant Green, R-Wellston, and signed by Gov. Kevin Stitt. The law took effect July 1. It defines "large load customers" as new facilities adding 75 megawatts or more of demand — sweeping in data centers, AI facilities and cryptocurrency mining operations — and requires them to cover their share of electricity and infrastructure costs so families, small businesses and traditional industrial customers are not left carrying them. Developers must notify adjoining landowners, county commissioners and the Oklahoma Corporation Commission within 60 days of acquiring land for a qualifying project.

videos.title: Oklahoma senator seeks interim study on data centers
videos.description:
An Oklahoma State Senator has proposed an interim study to take a closer look at the impact data centers could have on the state of Oklahoma.

Interim studies provide lawmakers an opportunity to study issues outside of the legislative session.

State Sen. Kendal Sacchieri (R-Blanchard) ran a bill last legislative session to put a moratorium on the construction of new data centers in Oklahoma until November of 2029.

That legislation did not make it across the finish line. Sacchieri told FOX 25 she felt an interim study might be the best way to bring more attention to the issue to then get better a better piece of legislation ready for next session.

"Data Centers and what all they mean for our state" is the title of the interim study Sacchieri has proposed.

"I'm open to both sides coming. We have had a few interim studies. Most of them I would say has been a one-sided bringing in the industry and talking about just... being a large load consumer and talking on the energy side," Sacchieri said.

Sacchieri told FOX 25 she would like to bring in industrial hygienists for the study.

"I would like to bring those kinds of professionals in and then if it would be best to have them and then the other side there with them to hash it out, I'm fine with that," she said. "I just want to make sure that we're bringing in not just the industry anymore. We want to bring in those that are professionally been through chemistry and understand what is going into our water system and how these closed loop systems work, etc."

The State Senator said the concerns she is hearing about data centers go even beyond water and energy.

"Citizens' concerns are just what's this going to do to my livelihood? So a lot of it is property value. We have not had these things around homes long enough," Sacchieri said. "People are concerned for their livestock, expecting mothers, noise pollution, noise, you know, what is this noise doing alone to my livelihood? And then of course it comes down to the water. Is this water still, you know, perfectly fine to drink and take and use once it's dumped into wastewater somewhere else down the road wherever, you know, these data centers are putting them, lakes, waters, creeks, whatever."

Sacchieri said she may even bring in the Oklahoma Corporation Commission to ask them some questions.

"How much have you really monitored these data centers since they've been here? 'Cause we've had some here for a very long time. How much wastewater is Google dumping daily? Are you monitoring what is in this wastewater," Sacchieri said.

Sacchieri could use the interim study to see what potential legislation needs to be considered during the next legislative session.

"Maybe we need to look at within a radius, if we can monitor their water usage and there is chemicals in these water when they're putting it back into the system, just the water system itself, they may have to chime in and help these local jurisdictions that currently don't have a proper waste management system, don't have the way to get these PFAS back out of the water whenever they have to treat it," she said.

The Senate Pro Tem has approved this interim study. The Agriculture and Wildlife Committee Chairman will also have to consider it and then schedule it.

Interim studies must be completed by October 30.

"The demand for electricity on our grid continues to grow. Our goal in the legislature is to put some guardrails in place and state law, that way we put some ratepayer protections in place," said State Rep. Brad Boles, the law's author.

Rep. Boles told FOX 25 his constituents have been very vocal and very concerned about data centers, but how exactly will the legislation make sure that Oklahoma ratepayers don't bare the brunt of these data centers? Boles said the Oklahoma Corporation Commission is a key piece to all of this.

"What the Corporation Commission does is reviews those costs and make sure that its fair and reasonable and just, and in this situation, we're going to make sure that, at least state law will direct the commission to basically say 'If it's a large load user, we got to make sure that they pay for all their cost,'" he said.

Rep. Boles said this applies to new data centers and wouldn't impact ones that are already up and running. The law also requires a 10 year service commitment and regulates 75 megawatt centers.

FOX 25 asked if there's any way companies could dance around that requirement.

"Yeah, could they try to build multiple locations of 70 megawatt? Potentially. But it would end up costing more doing that than just paying for the infrastructure cost," he said.

Rep. Boles said the law will go into effect July 1st, now that Governor Stitt has signed off on it.

videos.title: Claremore residents speak out against Project Mustang data center
videos.description:
CLAREMORE, OKLA. (KTUL) — Claremore city officials have known about Project Mustang, a new data center, for the past several months, but residents just found out in the past few days.

"You’re not a good community partner by surprising everybody," said Kelly Boegemann, who has been so concerned about the spread of data centers that she started an online petition to keep them out of Rogers County before she even knew about Project Mustang.

"I saw what was happening in other counties and communities, and I didn’t want that to happen to us," she said.

Project Mustang is being spearheaded by Beale, the same company behind Project Atlas in Coweta, which has seen a strong outpouring of public opposition.

"Citizens all around Oklahoma have said bluntly that we don’t want these data centers here. There’ve been protests, we’ve told elected officials over and over and over again, and it all comes down to money. They’re not listening to us, and that’s the problem," said Claremore resident Payton Pepin, who is running for state senate.

"We feel like this was not done in good faith, a lot of these have not been done in good faith, they’ve kept them secret, and we feel like they’ve tried to rip us off," he said.

The data center would be located at Claremore Industrial Park, with the first phase targeted for a 2028 completion. The city released a statement saying in part, “The City, in partnership with Claremore Economic Development, has an established history of advancing industrial projects in a manner that safeguards public interests and supports long-term community sustainability.”

"I’m against it," said Lane Brown, who is running for District 1 Rogers County commissioner.

"If it was truly economic development, we’d be open and transparent about this, we’d be like, 'Hey, let’s do this, this is good for the community,' but it’s not. They’re secretly doing this stuff," he said.

A new year, a new controversy over data centers, but the message from some residents is a very familiar tune.

"I guess my point is, and what I’d really like the data centers to know is that we don’t want you here, please don’t come," said Pepin.

Full Statement from City of Claremore

"The City of Claremore and Claremore Economic Development (CED) have taken a long-term, strategic approach to industrial planning, recognizing that large-scale infrastructure projects require extensive planning, coordination and foresight. Since 2013, CED has strategically acquired land in and around the Claremore Industrial Park to enable long-term planning, attract top employers and ensure projects align with zoning, land-use and fiscal standards.

"Over the past several months, the City and CED have been engaged in discussions regarding a potential large-scale economic development project, known as Project Mustang, within the Claremore Industrial Park. As with all industrial projects, rigorous site due diligence is required to determine feasibility before any commitments are made. As this due diligence phase nears completion, the project would move toward consideration of a Tax Increment District (TID) process prior to any land closing.

"The proposed project would be located on land already zoned for industrial use and would not increase existing local tax rates or utility rates. As an air-cooled facility, it would have limited impact on Claremore’s water supply and all required initial infrastructure upgrades would be paid for by the developer. The City and CED have been informed that the project owner/developer and end-user are domestically owned and publicly traded companies.

"The City, in partnership with Claremore Economic Development, has an established history of advancing industrial projects in a manner that safeguards public interests and supports long-term community sustainability,” said John Feary, Claremore City Manager. “All projects are governed by public oversight, enforceable contractual protections and strict adherence to all applicable local, state and federal regulations for the protection of residents, ratepayers and the community as a whole."

videos.title: Minnesota City Council Fled the Room Before a Data Center Vote
videos.description:
In Inver Grove Heights, Minnesota, the city council adjourned before a scheduled data center vote as 80+ residents booed. That's one of eight stories unfolding across America right now.

🏘️ **COMMUNITY** — The Inver Grove Heights, MN City Council adjourned Monday night before a scheduled data center moratorium vote, prompting boos and shouting from 80+ residents. The hearing was rescheduled for Friday at 8 AM. Council Member Sue Gliva cited unspecified "confidential" new information. The developer behind the proposed 54,000 sq ft facility has threatened legal action if the city acts on anything beyond zoning law.

🗳️ **LEGAL** — In Frederick County, Maryland, the Frederick County Data Center Referendum Committee filed its opening appeal brief with the Maryland Supreme Court on Tuesday, representing 21,000+ residents who signed a petition to vote on a 2,615-acre data center zone north of Adamstown. A lower court blocked the referendum. Oral arguments are set June 30 — one day before ballot language is due to the state.

⚖️ **LEGAL** — 1000 Friends of Oregon, Tax Fairness Oregon, the Tualatin Riverkeepers, and a sitting Hillsboro City Councilor sued Hillsboro and Washington County Monday over tax breaks for 17 data centers. The city rushed enterprise zone approvals to beat Oregon's June 6 data center tax moratorium. The Oregon Education Association is also a plaintiff.

⚡ **POWER** — A new Cleanview analysis reveals 46 planned U.S. data centers with 56 GW combined capacity plan to build private gas plants and bypass the grid entirely. That sidesteps utility regulators — while leaving all ratepayers to fund grid upgrades. Residential electricity prices rose 11.5% in 2025; analysts forecast a further 40% increase by 2030.

💧 **WATER** — Two-thirds of 809 planned U.S. data centers are being sited in drought-affected areas (Tom's Hardware / The Guardian). AI data centers consumed 264 billion gallons of water in 2025 — 550 million gallons per day. U.S. data center water demand is forecast to quadruple by 2028, reaching 73 billion gallons per year.

🏛️ **POLICY** — Florida Governor DeSantis signed SB 484 (effective July 1): data centers drawing 50 MW or more must pay their full cost of service, including all grid upgrades. Utilities are barred from charging residential or small-business ratepayers for data center infrastructure. At least 12 other states are pursuing similar laws.

🏗️ **NEW BUILD** — Miami developer Revitalization Unlimited filed plans for a 20-story, 384-foot data center tower in downtown Kansas City, designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill. The 140,880 sq ft building devotes 18 floors to IT racks and fuel cells, with a coffee shop on the ground floor. City review begins June 30.

💰 **INVESTMENT** — Australia-based IREN's "Project Emerald" — a 2,000-acre hyperscale AI campus in Pittsburg County, Oklahoma — was stalled Monday when county commissioners tabled two proposed tax incentive districts. 200 residents showed up opposed; one called it "a tax avoidance structure written by the developer's attorneys." videos.description:
Nine hundred Utahns showed up to a county commission hearing and forced Kevin O'Leary's city-sized data center into a 75% scale-back — and it's now a national story that Congress is watching. Here's everything happening in U.S. data centers right now.

🏘️ **COMMUNITY** — Utah's proposed 40,000-acre Stratos Project in Box Elder County was set to consume 9 gigawatts of electricity — more than double the entire state's usage. Over 900 people packed the county hearing, 300 more rallied outside, and investor Kevin O'Leary admitted "We pissed off a lot of people." He agreed to a 75% scale-back. Congress held hearings on June 11 as the protests went national. Residents cite threats to the Great Salt Lake's water supply.

⚖️ **LEGAL** — New York's legislature passed the Responsible Data Center Development Act (S10642) in a historic vote: Senate 44-16, Assembly 102-39. If signed by Gov. Kathy Hochul, New York would become the first state in the nation to impose a statewide moratorium on large data center permits. The one-year ban would freeze new environmental approvals for any facility drawing 20 megawatts or more. Hochul has not committed to signing.

⚡ **POWER/REGULATORY** — Ohio lawmakers unveiled what may be the nation's most sweeping data center regulation bill, targeting tax incentive rollbacks, nondisclosure agreement bans, water use reporting, and ratepayer billing protections in a single package. A separate citizen petition is circulating for a constitutional amendment to ban large-scale data centers in Ohio. Five other Heartland states — Illinois, Iowa, Minnesota, Oklahoma, and Wisconsin — are advancing similar legislation.

videos.title: Data centers aplenty in Muskogee County
videos.description:
MUSKOGEE, (Okla.) — The Muskogee area is no stranger to data centers. There's the up and running Polaris Technology, and just across the street is the under-construction Project Scissortail data center. And this week, an announcement by Google that two new data centers are being planned for Muskogee County as well.

"There's activity happening in the city where there really has been no major job creation in over 20 years," said local entrepreneur Charles Crawford. He's running for city council and says the construction boom has been great for his bed and breakfast.

"My bed and breakfast and my Airbnbs are doing fantastic with the increased labor force coming here, and that is the good side of all this is there’s jobs coming here," he said.

Noticeably absent in Muskogee, any large-scale organized resistance to data centers as recently seen in Coweta.

But that's not to say that concerns about water usage and power rates are absent here.

"The cautious tale is can you do it and still protect the small farmers, still protect the river the streams out there and protect the watershed and keep enough power and electricity available for the 37,000 people that live in this community," he said.

Google says when it comes to power, it "will add 600 megawatts (MW) of new clean energy to Oklahoma’s electricity grid," from nearby solar farms. And as for water, "The company is supporting a regenerative agriculture program that seeks to replenish approximately 1.4 billion gallons of water in North-Central Oklahoma over the next seven years."

Assurances that only go so far with some residents worried about rate hikes.

"There are people here who are living paycheck to paycheck. I think we have almost 25% of our population just in the city of Muskogee is considered poverty and every penny they’ve got to account for," said concerned resident Mark Hughes.

The data center boom of Muskogee County, arriving at the speed of tech, with misgivings by some as to benefits they'll actually create.

"There are two things I don't trust, the government and big corporations," said Hughes.

This Real Talk will bring together local advocates, journalists, and tech industry professionals, going beyond the headlines to have a informed and balanced discussion about the potential impact – good and bad – of data centers in Oklahoma. 

Oklahoma has a long history of being friendly to extractive economies such as oil and natural gas. Once described as the “Oil Capital of the World,” Tulsa, OK’s Mid-Continent field provided more than 35% of the petroleum produced in the entire United States by 1916. The petroleum industry has been the primary driver of the state’s economy for the entirety of the 20th century. Today, the state is struggling to find its relevance and identity in the midst of changing cultures, economies, and technology.

Hyperscale data centers create massive amounts of demand for land, water, energy, and early reporting from places like Memphis, TN and Atlanta, GA (South Fulton) point to Black and brown communities suffering the greatest negative effects of these developments.

Project Anthem is a 340 acre development that will include a hyperscale data center which will be built near 11th Street and the Creek Turnpike in Tulsa, OK on land that is currently owned by the City of Tulsa. The project was announced as a partnership with the City and a company called Atmoss LLC. It is largely believed that Atmoss is associated with Meta, the parent company of Facebook.

Project Clydesdale is another hyperscale datacenter project being built on about 500 acres on 76th Street N and North Sheridan Road in Tulsa County, near the city of Owasso. What's the true cost of the AI revolution and who should be paying for it? We went to Georgia to find out. 

Demand for data centers is booming as ChatGPT and other AI tools become integrated into our daily life. Under the Trump administration, investments into data centers in the U.S. is expected to surpass $1 trillion in the next five years.

But data centers put extraordinary demand on the power grid and require entirely new infrastructure. In the next three years, data center use of electricity is expected to double or even triple.

We went to rural Georgia, the state with the fastest data center growth in the country, and spoke with residents who are living next to massive data centers owned by Meta and Blackstone and facing nonstop noise, pollution and rapidly rising electricity bills.
